section.title: Paul before Agrippa
section.sectionRationale: This is the fullest and most personal of Paul's defenses, delivered before a Jewish king who knows the Scriptures. Paul retells his conversion and commission on the Damascus road, presses the risen Christ upon Agrippa from Moses and the Prophets, and turns the dock into a pulpit. It is the climactic testimony of Acts, the gospel proclaimed to the highest rank Paul has yet faced.
section.thesis: Standing in chains before a king, Paul tells how the risen Jesus met him, turned a persecutor into a witness, and sent him to open blind eyes among Jew and Gentile; and he begs even his judges to believe the prophets and become what he is, minus only the chains.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Paul's respectful opening and his hope in God's promise; his account of persecuting the church and meeting the risen Christ on the Damascus road; his faithful obedience to the heavenly vision, preaching light to Jew and Gentile; and the exchange with Festus and Agrippa that ends in a verdict of innocence.

units.label: Paul's opening and his hope
units.note: on trial for the promise made to the fathers

verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense:
“King Agrippa, I consider myself fortunate to stand before you today to defend myself against all the accusations of the Jews,
especially since you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies. I beg you, therefore, to listen to me patiently.
Surely all the Jews know how I have lived from my earliest childhood among my own people, and also in Jerusalem.
They have known me for a long time and can testify, if they are willing, that I lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion.
And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers,
the promise our twelve tribes are hoping to see fulfilled as they earnestly serve God day and night. It is because of this hope, O king, that I am accused by the Jews.
Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?

units.label: The persecutor meets the risen Christ
units.note: Saul, why do you persecute Me

verses.text: So then, I too was convinced that I ought to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I put many of the saints in prison, and when they were condemned to death, I cast my vote against them.
I frequently had them punished in the synagogues, and I tried to make them blaspheme. In my raging fury against them, I even went to foreign cities to persecute them.
In this pursuit I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests.
About noon, O king, as I was on the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and my companions.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice say to me in Hebrew, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the {{kentron|goads}}.’
‘Who are You, Lord?’ I asked. ‘I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,’ the Lord replied.
‘But get up and stand on your feet. For I have appeared to you to appoint you as a servant and as a {{martys|witness}} of what you have seen from Me and what I will show you.
I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them

to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in Me.’

units.label: Not disobedient to the vision
units.note: light to our people and to the Gentiles

verses.text: So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.

First to those in Damascus and Jerusalem, then to everyone in the region of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, I declared that they should {{metanoeo|repent}} and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of their repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple courts and tried to kill me.
But I have had God’s help to this day, and I stand here to testify to small and great alike. I am saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen:
that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.”

units.label: Almost persuaded
units.note: would to God you were as I am, except these chains

verses.text: At this stage of Paul’s defense, Festus exclaimed in a loud voice, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!”
But Paul answered, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety.
For the king knows about these matters, and I can speak freely to him. I am confident that none of this has escaped his notice, because it was not done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do.”
Then Agrippa said to Paul, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a {{christianos|Christian}}?”
“Short time or long,” Paul replied, “I wish to God that not only you but all who hear me this day may become what I am, except for these chains.”
Then the king and the governor rose, along with Bernice and those seated with them.
On their way out, they said to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.”

kentron.gloss: A goad, the sharp point used to drive oxen; also a sting. To kick against the goads was a proverb for fighting a stronger power to one's own hurt. The risen Christ tells Saul that his fierce campaign has really been a futile struggle against God, wounding only himself.

martys.gloss: A witness, one who testifies to what he has seen. Christ appoints Paul a martys of the risen Lord, the very calling given to the apostles in Acts 1:8. From this word comes martyr, for faithful witness would cost many their lives; Paul's whole ministry is summed up as bearing witness to Jesus.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, literally to change one's mind, a turning of the whole person from sin to God. Paul's message everywhere is that people should repent and turn to God and show it by their deeds. Repentance is not mere regret but a reorientation of life that follows the opening of blind eyes.

christianos.gloss: A Christian, one belonging to Christ; a name first given at Antioch, Acts 11:26. Agrippa uses it half in irony, asking whether Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly. Paul takes the word in earnest and wishes all his hearers were as he is, except for his chains.

basic.context: Festus has arranged for Paul to speak before King Agrippa, an expert in Jewish matters, so he can frame the charges for Caesar. Given the floor, Paul delivers the longest and most personal of his defenses. He describes his zealous past as a persecutor, tells how the risen Jesus stopped him on the Damascus road and commissioned him, and then appeals directly to Agrippa to believe the Scriptures and the risen Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as testimony that becomes evangelism. Paul moves from his life story to the Damascus-road encounter to a direct gospel appeal. Watch how the defense quietly puts the king on trial: by the end it is Agrippa, not Paul, who must decide what to do with the risen Jesus and the prophets he claims to believe.
basic.originalLanguages: Christ tells Saul it is hard to kick against the kentron, the goads, resisting God only wounds himself. He appoints Paul a martys, a witness, of the risen Lord. Paul's message is that all should metanoeo, repent, and turn to God. And Agrippa asks whether Paul would so quickly make him a Christianos, a Christian.
basic.typology: The suffering and rising Christ Paul preaches is the fulfillment of Moses and the Prophets: the Messiah must suffer, be the first to rise, and bring light to the nations. Paul's commission to open blind eyes and turn people from darkness to light echoes the servant of Isaiah, a light for the Gentiles.
basic.christ: The risen Jesus is the whole content of Paul's defense. He appears in blazing light, names Himself, and sends Paul to the nations. The gospel Paul preaches is exactly this: the Christ would suffer, rise first from the dead, and proclaim light to Jew and Gentile. The persecuted one is the reigning Lord.
basic.god: God had promised light for the nations through Israel, and here that promise is being fulfilled. The same God who made the promise to the fathers now sends Paul to open Gentile eyes. God's help sustains His witness to this day, and God's purpose cannot be stopped by prison or a king's hesitation.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 9 and 22 give the other two accounts of the Damascus road. Isaiah 42 speaks of the servant as a light to the Gentiles. Acts 1:8 sets out the call to be witnesses. Luke 24:46 to 47 states the pattern: the Christ must suffer, rise, and repentance be preached to all nations.
basic.oneStory: The commission Paul received is the mission of the whole book: from Jerusalem the risen Christ sends His witnesses to open the eyes of the nations. Standing before a king, Paul embodies that mission, preaching light to Jew and Gentile and pleading for all to turn and believe.

context.literary:
Acts 26 is shaped like a formal speech of defense, and Luke gives it the classical parts: a courteous opening in verses 2 and 3, a statement of Paul's earlier life in verses 4 to 11, the main narrative of the vision in verses 12 to 18, an account of his obedience and its results in verses 19 to 23, and an appeal in verses 24 to 29. Within this order there is a steady turn. The speech begins with Paul's defense against the Jews' accusations and ends with Paul questioning the king. The defendant becomes the evangelist and the judge becomes the hearer.

The center is the vision, and its center is the commission in verses 16 to 18. Notice how the sentences of Jesus rise in length and weight: a rebuke, a name, a command to stand, and then a long sentence of purpose that sends Paul to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light, and bring them forgiveness and an inheritance. Luke gives more of Jesus' words here than in the other two tellings, Acts 9 and 22, and leaves out Ananias altogether. Paul, speaking to a king, goes straight to the commission, because it is the commission that explains why he is on trial.

Verses 6 to 8 form a quiet frame around the whole speech. Paul says he is on trial for the hope of the promise made to the fathers, and he asks, 'Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?' Then verse 23 returns to the same subject with the resurrection of the Christ. The beginning and the end enclose the story of Paul's conversion with the question that governed all of his trials.

The scene ends with three interruptions that Luke arranges like a descending staircase of response. Festus shouts that Paul is mad, verse 24; Agrippa asks whether Paul thinks he can persuade him in a short time, verse 28; and the whole company agrees that Paul has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment, verse 31. The speech closes on a verdict of innocence and a missed chance.
context.historical:
Marcus Julius Agrippa, Agrippa II, was a great-grandson of Herod the Great and the son of the Agrippa who killed James, Acts 12:1 to 2. He ruled lands to the north and east of Galilee by Rome's favor and had been given care of the temple and a say in the appointment of the high priests. This is why Paul calls him an expert in Jewish customs and controversies in verse 3 and why Festus, who is not, asks him to help frame the charges. His sister Bernice sits beside him. The audience hall in Caesarea was packed with the city's leaders, and the hearing was a state occasion.

Paul speaks as a former persecutor who knew the system from inside. Verses 9 to 11 describe a man acting with authority from the chief priests, casting his vote against the saints when they were condemned to death, forcing them to blaspheme, and pursuing them in foreign cities. The picture matches what Paul says of himself in 1 Timothy 1:13 and Galatians 1:13. It is a sober account of a man who believed he was serving God.

The voice from heaven speaks in Hebrew, that is, the Hebrew language of the Jews, probably Aramaic, as the BSB note says. Jesus also says 'it is hard for you to kick against the goads.' The goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen, and kicking against it only hurt the animal. The saying was a familiar one in Greek literature, and a Greek-speaking king would have recognized it. It does not appear in the account of Acts 22.

The date is around AD 59 or 60. Paul's reference to 'twelve tribes' in verse 7 shows that Jews in the first century still thought of themselves as a people with a shared hope, and the 'promise made to our fathers' is the covenant with Abraham and David. The mention of Moses and the prophets in verse 22 is also historically precise: the Jewish Scriptures gave the framework within which a Jewish king, and in a different way a Roman governor, could understand the claim that the Messiah would suffer and rise.
context.canonical:
Paul's account of his commission is built from Old Testament calls. When Jesus says in verse 16, get up and stand on your feet, He speaks as God spoke to Ezekiel, who was told to stand up on his feet so that God could speak to him, Ezekiel 2:1 to 3. The promise to rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles in verse 17 is the promise God gave Jeremiah when He sent him, do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, Jeremiah 1:7 to 8. Paul is placed among the prophets.

The purpose clauses in verse 18 come from Isaiah. The Servant is appointed as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and to bring prisoners out of darkness, Isaiah 42:6 to 7, and he is told that it is not enough to raise the tribes of Jacob, for he will bring salvation to the ends of the earth, Isaiah 49:6. In Acts 13:47 Paul and Barnabas had already applied this to their mission. Here the risen Jesus gives His own mission, the Servant's mission, to His apostle.

The core of the message in verses 22 and 23, that the Christ would suffer, be the first to rise from the dead and proclaim light to Jews and Gentiles, is the pattern Jesus taught on the Emmaus road and in the upper room, Luke 24:25 to 27 and 24:44 to 47. It joins the suffering and glory of the Messiah, Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53, with the resurrection and the mission to the nations.

Finally, the chapter belongs to the series of accounts of Paul's conversion, Acts 9, 22 and 26, and to Paul's own retellings, Galatians 1:15 to 16 and 1 Corinthians 15:8. Each emphasizes something different: the event in Acts 9, the testimony to a Jewish crowd in Acts 22, and the commission before a king here. The accounts agree on the center: the risen Jesus appeared to a persecutor and made him a witness. The attention Luke gives to this story shows that it was foundational for the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers to see that the Christian message is not a break from Israel's faith but its fulfillment. Paul says in verse 22 that he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen, and in verses 6 to 8 that the hope on which he is judged is the hope of the twelve tribes. The reader is meant to leave convinced that to follow Jesus is to follow the Scriptures to their goal.

He also means to show the character of a faithful witness. Paul speaks with honesty about his own past, including cruelty, with clarity about the one who stopped him, and with warmth towards those who hear. His closing wish, that all who hear him may become what he is except for the chains, is the heart of an evangelist who wants his judges saved more than he wants himself acquitted.

Finally, Luke puts the reader in Agrippa's seat. The king is asked a direct question, do you believe the prophets, and given no way of avoiding it. Everyone who reads Acts 26 is brought to the same point. The question is not whether Paul's story is interesting but whether the risen Jesus is who He said He is, and what a person should do about it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The story of the Damascus road is a unique event. No one else is struck by a light brighter than the sun and called by name from heaven to be an apostle. The passage describes an unrepeatable moment in the founding of the church, and believers should not expect to copy its form. What can be shared is its pattern: the risen Christ finds enemies, forgives them and sends them out.

The specific commission in verses 17 and 18 was given to Paul for the Gentile mission, and yet its purposes describe what every believer's witness aims at. People are blind and need their eyes opened, they are in darkness and need light, they are under the power of Satan and need to come to God, and they need forgiveness and a place among the sanctified. The apostolic office does not pass to us, but the message and the aim do.

Paul's appeal to Agrippa is a model of how to speak to someone in power: respectful, personal, grounded in what the listener already knows, and plain about what he is asking. His wish in verse 29 describes his heart, not a rule. It would be a mistake to turn it into a method. What Paul offers is a witness that cares about the listener's salvation more than the speaker's comfort, and it is that spirit that the passage sets before us.

debates.question: Was the Damascus road primarily Paul's conversion or his prophetic commissioning?

views.label: A conversion from sin to faith
views.case: Paul was a persecutor who met Jesus and was changed. He calls himself the worst of sinners in 1 Timothy 1:13 to 16 and says he was shown mercy. Verse 18 speaks of forgiveness of sins and turning from darkness to light, the language of conversion.

views.label: A call like the call of a prophet
views.case: Paul does not speak of a change of religion. He describes Jesus appearing to appoint him as servant and witness, in terms that echo Ezekiel and Jeremiah, and in Galatians 1:15 he speaks of being set apart from his mother's womb. Some readers prefer to say that Paul remained a faithful Jew who received a calling.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Luke and Paul give the encounter both aspects: forgiveness and a mission. Since the one who appears is the risen Christ, to meet Him is to be turned and to be sent. Paul would not have seen these as separate.

debates.bearing: The passage gives enough to affirm both. The first thing Paul tells Agrippa is his zeal against Jesus; the last is his obedience to the heavenly vision. For readers the point is that meeting Christ never ends with a private change; it makes the forgiven a messenger.

debates.question: What did Agrippa mean in verse 28?

views.label: A sincere moved reply
views.case: The BSB reads, 'Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?' On this view the king is touched and wonders aloud how far he is being drawn. Paul's reply, which wishes that all who hear might be like him, takes the remark seriously.

views.label: A sarcastic deflection
views.case: Others read it as a polite rebuff, as in 'You think that with so little effort you can make me a Christian?' The title Christianos may have been a term of scorn among outsiders, and Agrippa could be keeping his distance from it.

views.label: A careful non-answer
views.case: A diplomat in a public setting might say something deliberately open to both readings. The Greek is difficult, and the phrase en oligo, in little, could mean in a short time or with little effort.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity is perhaps intended. Luke leaves the king's heart unrecorded, so that each reader supplies the answer to the question Paul has put in verse 27. Whatever Agrippa meant, Paul's reply shows how a believer ought to respond to a hesitant listener: with warmth, with honesty about the cost, and with no resentment.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's Greek in this chapter carries more than the English shows. In verse 8 he asks why it should be judged incredible, apiston krinetai, that God raises the dead. The word apiston is the negative of pistis, faith, so it means unbelievable, and Paul's question presses the audience: the problem is not the evidence but the assumption that God cannot act. The Greek verb is in the present, God raises the dead, which makes the claim about the character of God rather than a single event.

In verse 16 Jesus says He has appeared to Paul to appoint him, procheirisasthai, a hand-picked choice. The same verb is used of Ananias in Acts 22:14 and of the Messiah appointed in Acts 3:20, and the word suggests God taking someone into His own hand for a task. Paul becomes a hyperetes, a servant, literally an under-rower or attendant who serves another's command, and a martys, a witness. The first word is humble and the second is public. He is to witness to what he has seen and to what Jesus will yet show him, so that the witness includes things still to come.

The commission has four verbs of movement: to open, anoixai, their eyes; to turn, epistrepsai, from darkness to light; and then to receive forgiveness, aphesis, and a place among the sanctified. The word for inheritance, kleros, is a portion or lot, the language used of Israel's share in the land. Gentiles are to receive a share among those set apart by faith in Jesus. In verse 20 Paul says he called people to repent and turn, metanoein and epistrephein, and to perform deeds worthy of repentance, an insistence that real turning shows itself in life.

In verse 19 Paul says he was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, optasia. The word is used for a sight or appearance, as in Luke 1:22 and 24:23 and 2 Corinthians 12:1. Paul does not claim that an experience made him special; he says he obeyed what he saw.

The speech ends in a clash of words. Festus shouts mainē, you are mad. The same verb is used by the household in Acts 12:15 when they tell Rhoda she is out of her mind for saying that Peter is at the door. In both cases, the news is too good or too strange to be true. Paul answers that he speaks words of truth and sobriety, aletheias kai sophrosynes, a pairing of truth with sound-mindedness, the opposite of madness. In verse 26 he says that none of this was done en gonia, in a corner. The point is that the events were public and checkable, and a king should know them.

Agrippa's reply, en oligo me peitheis Christianon poiesai, is hard to translate, which is why renderings differ. Paul's answer uses the same phrase, en oligo kai en megalo, 'in little or in much', and adds that he wishes his hearers would become as he is. The word desmos, chains, appears last, as a sober exception. The man who is bound is the freest person in the room.

typology.type: The Servant who is a light to the nations, Isaiah 42:6 to 7 and 49:6
typology.fulfillment: Jesus' commission in verse 18, to open eyes and turn from darkness to light, uses the Servant's task. In Isaiah the Servant is given as a light to the nations and to bring prisoners from the dungeon. Jesus is that Servant, Luke 2:32, and in Acts 13:47 Paul and Barnabas take the words as their own mission. The escalation is that the Servant who was promised now sends His witnesses to carry the light. The type falls short in that Paul is not the Servant; he is a servant of the Servant, and the light is Christ's, not his.

typology.type: The suffering and rising Messiah of Moses and the Prophets, verses 22 and 23
typology.fulfillment: Paul says he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen, that the Christ would suffer and be the first to rise. The pattern is Isaac bound and returned, Genesis 22; Joseph from the pit to the throne, Genesis 41; the Servant of Isaiah 53 who is pierced and then sees light and is satisfied, Isaiah 53:10 to 12; and the holy one of Psalm 16:10 not left to decay. Jesus Himself taught this pattern in Luke 24:25 to 27. The pictures fall short individually, and only in Christ do they meet.

typology.type: The prophet called and sent, Ezekiel 2:1 to 3 and Jeremiah 1:7 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Jesus' words to Paul to stand up and go echo what God said to Ezekiel and Jeremiah. Like them, Paul is sent to people who may not listen, promised rescue and given words to speak. The escalation is that the one who commissions now is the risen Lord, and the mission reaches the Gentiles. Paul's calling is more than prophetic, because he is an apostle commissioned directly by the risen Christ, Galatians 1:1. The type falls short in that the prophets spoke of a day to come, whereas Paul speaks of a day that has begun.

The man who set out to arrest believers is arrested by the Lord. There is a pattern in Scripture of God turning His opponents into servants, as with Jonah, who fled, and the Gentile nations that would one day worship, Isaiah 19:24 to 25. The fullness is that Paul becomes the pattern for all sinners, as he says in 1 Timothy 1:16, an example of the Lord's patience. The pattern falls short if it is read as a formula, since not every conversion looks like this.

study.christ:
In verse 15 Paul asks, who are You, Lord, and the answer is, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Everything in the chapter rests on that answer. The person who speaks from heaven is the same Jesus who was crucified in Jerusalem, and He is alive, glorious and in command. A persecutor discovers that the man he thought was dead is the Lord, and that to attack the church is to attack Him. The unity of Christ with His people is part of the gospel here, and it is stated in His own words.

The summary in verse 23 is the clearest account of the Messiah in the speech: that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles. Three things are said of Him. He suffers, and Luke uses a word that describes him as one destined to suffer. He rises first, which means that others will follow, as Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:20. And He proclaims light, which He does through the apostles, as Luke 24:47 and Acts 1:8 say. The risen Lord is still the one proclaiming; His witnesses are the means.

The commission in verses 17 and 18 depicts what Christ does. He opens eyes, which in the Gospels is something He does for the blind. He turns people from darkness to light, from the power of Satan to God. He gives forgiveness of sins and an inheritance. Each of these is work that belongs to Him alone. Paul is the messenger, but the effects are Christ's: faith in Me, as Jesus says at the end of verse 18. It is faith in Jesus that sanctifies. The message does not point to Paul's own authority or experience, but to a person.

There is a further link between Jesus and the one who stands before the king. The Lord said, I will rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles, verse 17, and in verse 22 Paul says, I have had God's help to this day. The risen Christ keeps His promises to His servant even when the servant stands in chains. He is not only the content of the message but the keeper of the messenger.

We should avoid forcing every detail into allegory. The goads are not a symbol of the cross, and the light is not simply the Servant of Isaiah. What the text allows us to say is that Moses, the prophets, and the Damascus road all point to the same person, and that He is alive. It is that person whom Agrippa is asked about when Paul says, do you believe the prophets? Believing the prophets, on Paul's reading, means believing in Jesus, since He is what they pointed toward.
study.god:
The God of this chapter keeps promises across centuries. Paul says that he is on trial because of his hope in the promise that God made to our fathers, verse 6, the promise that the twelve tribes hope to see fulfilled as they serve God day and night. The speech begins with a long memory. God made a promise to Abraham and David and to the prophets, and Paul is saying that the promise has been kept in Jesus. The chapter teaches us to read God's faithfulness at the scale of generations.

The God who makes such promises is also a God who acts in particular moments. A bright light at noon, a voice speaking in the language of the persecuted, a name used twice, and a command to stand: the God of Scripture is not a distant idea but one who meets people. He interrupts a man's plans to bring him to Himself. That is the same God who met Moses at the bush and Isaiah in the temple, and who now has met Paul through the risen Son.

God is also shown to be rich in mercy toward enemies. Paul describes his violence in detail, and the answer he receives is a commission rather than a sentence. The forgiveness of sins, which verse 18 lists among the gifts of the gospel, is the way God treats a man who has killed and imprisoned His people. This does not make light of sin. The text says plainly that Paul was raging against the saints. It shows a God whose patience is greater than the sinner's rage, as Paul himself later writes in 1 Timothy 1:16.

Third, the chapter shows God as the one who holds His servant. I have had God's help to this day, Paul says in verse 22. The help is not the removal of chains but the strength to testify to small and great alike. God's power is not in avoiding trouble but in sustaining witness through it. When Paul says that he is sober and speaking the truth, he is relying on a God whose truth does not need defense by cleverness.

For worship, this means that God is to be praised as the one who keeps old promises, meets people in their opposition, and sends the forgiven to others. It also means that God's purposes for the Gentiles were not an afterthought: the light to the nations, promised in Isaiah, is the plan from the start. The same God who set Paul apart from his mother's womb, Galatians 1:15, is the one who has set His love on the nations, and who calls every hearer, king or not, to turn and live.

crossReferences.note: This is the first telling of the Damascus road in Luke's own voice. In that account Ananias plays a large part, and Jesus' words to Paul are shorter. Comparing it with Acts 26 shows how Paul adapts the same event for a different audience, putting the commission from Jesus first when speaking to a king.

Here Paul tells the story to the Jerusalem crowd and stresses Ananias, a devout observer of the law, who tells him he will be a witness to everyone of what he has seen and heard. The three accounts agree on the center, the light and the voice, and differ in emphasis.

The LORD calls His Servant to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and bring prisoners out of the dungeon. These words stand behind Jesus' commission in verse 18, and show that Paul's mission is the Servant's mission carried forward.

It is not enough for the Servant to restore Israel, for He will also be a light for the nations, to bring salvation to the ends of the earth. Verse 23, which says the Christ will proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles, is a direct echo.

God tells Ezekiel to stand on his feet, and then sends him to a rebellious nation. Jesus' command to Paul in verse 16, get up and stand on your feet, uses the same posture, and the sending to a people who resist places Paul among the prophets.

The LORD tells Jeremiah not to be afraid of those to whom he is sent, because He is with him to deliver him. The promise in verse 17 that Jesus will rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles repeats this pattern of a call joined to protection.

The risen Jesus tells the disciples that everything written about Him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled, that the Christ will suffer and rise on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness will be proclaimed to all nations. Paul's summary in verses 22 and 23 is this teaching, passed on.

Jesus tells the apostles they will be His witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria and to the ends of the earth. Paul's own account of his preaching in verse 20, first in Damascus and Jerusalem, then Judea, then to the Gentiles, matches this order, and shows the commission fulfilled.

Paul says he was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor and a violent man, but was shown mercy because he acted in ignorance and unbelief. This is Paul's own verdict on the story he tells in verses 9 to 11, and it explains why he speaks of it without self-defense, as the story of what mercy did.

Paul writes that God set him apart from his mother's womb and was pleased to reveal His Son in him so that he might preach Him among the Gentiles. This gives his own inside view of the same event, and supports the idea that the Damascus road was a call as well as a conversion.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a promise that the whole earth will be blessed through one family, Genesis 12:3, and spends hundreds of pages on how that can happen when the family itself is blind. Acts 26 is a moment when the answer is spoken aloud before a king. The Servant promised by Isaiah, who is a light to the nations, has come, suffered and risen, and now sends His witnesses to the nations. Paul puts it in a sentence: that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles.

Notice who is being sent. Throughout the Old Testament, Israel's enemies are the nations and their kings. In this chapter, the man who was Israel's most zealous guardian against the new faith is sent by Jesus to the nations. This is a reversal on the scale of the whole Bible. The one who stood on the side of the wall that kept Gentiles out becomes the one who opens the door. In Ephesians 2:13 to 19 Paul says that those who were far off have been brought near, and the Damascus road is where that message starts to travel.

The chapter also continues the story of the persecuted righteous one. From Abel to the prophets to Jesus, God's chosen ones suffer at the hands of the very people they come to save. Paul here stands in that line. Yet this line is turned on its head: the persecutor is forgiven and made a witness, which is a small picture of the way the cross turns defeat into victory.

Look ahead. The commission in verse 18, forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among the sanctified, points to the end of the story. The inheritance is the new creation, where people from every nation stand before the throne, Revelation 7:9, and where the light that Isaiah promised no longer needs a sun, Revelation 21:23 to 24. In Acts, the road leads to Rome, but the commission aims further, at a day when the darkness will be gone and eyes that were once closed will see. Agrippa heard the first call; the invitation still stands, and the same question comes to every reader: do you believe the prophets?

quiz.q: What did the risen Jesus commission Paul to do?

options.text: To be a witness who would open blind eyes and turn Jew and Gentile from darkness to light.
options.note: Christ appoints Paul a servant and witness, sending him to open eyes and turn people to God, verses 16 to 18.

options.text: To rescue him from his enemies and keep him safe.
options.note: Christ does promise to rescue him, verse 17, but that is in service of the mission, not the commission itself.

options.text: To rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: Nothing of the kind is said; Paul is sent to the nations with the gospel, not to a building project.

options.text: To keep his new faith private and cause no trouble.
options.note: The opposite; he is publicly sent to Jew and Gentile as a witness to the risen Christ.

quiz.q: What does Christ mean by telling Saul it is hard to kick against the goads?

options.text: His fierce fight against Jesus is a futile struggle against God that only wounds himself.
options.note: The proverb pictures an ox harming itself by kicking the goad; Saul cannot defeat God by persecuting the church.

options.text: Saul has been feeling guilty and resisting his conscience.
options.note: There may be an inner struggle in view, but the saying is chiefly about the futility of fighting the living God.

options.text: Saul should stop traveling to distant cities.
options.note: It is not about his travels but about the hopelessness of opposing Christ.

options.text: Saul is being praised for his zeal.
options.note: It is a rebuke, not praise; his zeal has been aimed against God Himself.

quiz.q: What is the heart of the message Paul says he preaches from Moses and the Prophets?

options.text: That the Christ would suffer, rise first from the dead, and bring light to Jew and Gentile.
options.note: Paul states this as the sum of his message, verses 22 to 23, drawn straight from the Scriptures.

options.text: That people should repent and turn to God and do deeds worthy of repentance.
options.note: True and part of his preaching, verse 20, but the core content is the suffering and risen Christ for all peoples.

options.text: That Israel alone would be saved.
options.note: Paul insists the light is for the Gentiles too, not for Israel only.

options.text: That the Messiah would come only to reign, never to suffer.
options.note: Paul says the opposite: the Christ would suffer and be the first to rise.

quiz.q: How does Paul respond to Agrippa's question about becoming a Christian?

options.text: He earnestly wishes that Agrippa and all his hearers might become as he is, except for the chains.
options.note: Paul turns the king's half-ironic question into a heartfelt evangelistic longing, verse 29.

options.text: He appeals to Agrippa's belief in the prophets to persuade him.
options.note: He does appeal to the prophets, verse 27, but his direct answer is the longing that all would be saved.

options.text: He grows angry and rebukes the king for mocking him.
options.note: Paul is gracious, not angry; he responds with warmth and hope, not rebuke.

options.text: He agrees that conversion is impossible in so short a time.
options.note: He says the opposite, longing that short time or long, all might come to Christ.

quiz.q: What verdict did Agrippa and Festus reach about Paul?

options.text: That he had done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment.
options.note: As they left they agreed Paul was innocent, verses 31 to 32, one more declaration of the gospel's innocence.

options.text: That he could have been freed had he not appealed to Caesar.
options.note: Agrippa says this, verse 32, but it flows from the deeper verdict that Paul was innocent.

options.text: That he was guilty but deserved leniency.
options.note: They did not find him guilty at all; they judged him innocent of any crime.

options.text: That he was a dangerous revolutionary.
options.note: They concluded the opposite, that he had done nothing deserving punishment.

questions: The risen Christ met Paul while he was still an enemy and made him a witness. How does it encourage you that Jesus saves and calls people who once opposed Him?
Paul turned his defense into an appeal for others to believe. When you are asked about your faith, do you see it as a chance to bear witness rather than merely to protect yourself?
Christ sent Paul to open blind eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Whose eyes are you longing to see opened, and how might God use you in that?
Agrippa came close, yet stopped short of faith. Where are you tempted to remain almost persuaded rather than fully surrendered to Christ?
Paul could say he had not been disobedient to the heavenly vision. What has God clearly called you to that requires fresh obedience today?

translationNotes.note: The voice spoke in Hebrew, which a footnote notes may mean Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea. The proverb about kicking against the goads, the kentron, was widely known in the ancient world and pictures the futility of resisting a stronger power.

To open their eyes and turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God draws on the language of Isaiah's servant, a light for the Gentiles; the commission describes the effect of the gospel: sight, deliverance, forgiveness, and inheritance.

Agrippa's question is often rendered almost you persuade me to become a Christian, but the Greek more likely carries a note of irony, in such a short time. Either way Paul answers the words in deep earnest, longing for the king's salvation.
